# Thermodynamics and statistical mechanics {#sec-thermodynamics-statistical-mechanics}

Thermodynamics describes a macroscopic system in equilibrium by a handful of state variables, pressure, volume,
temperature, energy and entropy, and by the laws that relate their changes; it says nothing about atoms, and its
results hold for any system whatever its microscopic constitution. Statistical mechanics derives those laws by
treating the microscopic state as a random variable: an ensemble is a probability measure on the microstates, the
thermodynamic quantities are expectations, and the temperature is the Lagrange multiplier that fixes the mean
energy. This chapter develops both in six sections. Thermodynamics introduces state variables, the first and second
laws, entropy, the thermodynamic potentials and the Maxwell relations, with the Carnot cycle as the running example.
Statistical ensembles defines the microcanonical, canonical and grand-canonical ensembles, the partition function and
the Boltzmann distribution, building on the probability spaces of @sec-probability-spaces. Partition functions of
simple systems computes the two-level system, the harmonic oscillator and the classical ideal gas exactly, and
proves equipartition. Quantum statistics derives the Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions, Planck's law of
blackbody radiation and, in outline, Bose-Einstein condensation. Phase transitions and Landau theory introduces
order parameters, the Landau free energy, spontaneous symmetry breaking, mean field theory and critical exponents,
and solves two spin systems exactly, the Curie-Weiss model and the Gaussian free field.
The last section shows that the partition function of a quantum system is a trace of $e^{-\beta H}$, an evolution in
imaginary time over an interval of length $\beta = 1/T$ whose ends are identified: finite temperature is a field
theory on a circle of circumference $\beta$, and the Fourier modes on that circle are the Matsubara frequencies.
Units: $k_B = 1$ throughout, so temperature is measured in energy units, and $\hbar = 1$ where quantum mechanics
enters, unless numbers in SI units are given. Every statement is followed by three examples of increasing complexity
and three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions, and the results are checked by exact
computation in Sage.

## Thermodynamics {#sec-thermodynamics}

Thermodynamics is the theory of equilibrium states of macroscopic systems and of the energy exchanged between them
as heat and work. This section defines the thermodynamic state and its variables, states the first law (energy
conservation with heat included) and the second law (through entropy), introduces the thermodynamic potentials as
Legendre transforms of the energy, and derives the Maxwell relations from the symmetry of mixed second derivatives;
the ideal gas, the van der Waals gas and the Carnot cycle serve as worked examples throughout.

### State variables and equilibrium

A gas in a box left alone settles into a state that no longer changes and that is described by a few numbers, the
volume, the pressure, the temperature and the amount of substance. The definition below names such states and the
variables that describe them, and distinguishes the variables that scale with the size of the system from those
that do not.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-thermodynamic-state}
#### Thermodynamic state

A macroscopic system is in **thermodynamic equilibrium** when its macroscopic properties do not change in time and
there are no net flows of energy or matter through it. An equilibrium state is a **thermodynamic state**; it is
determined by a small number of **state variables**, such as the internal energy $U$, the volume $V$, the particle
number $N$, the pressure $p$, the temperature $T$ and the entropy $S$, any independent set of which (for a simple
fluid, two of them at fixed $N$) fixes all the others. A state variable is **extensive** if it doubles when two
identical copies of the system are joined ($U, V, N, S$) and **intensive** if it is unchanged ($p, T$ and the
chemical potential $\mu$). A relation $f(p, V, T, N) = 0$ between state variables valid in all equilibrium states of
a system is its **equation of state**. Two systems in contact that exchange energy reach a common equilibrium, and
the **zeroth law** states that thermal equilibrium is transitive; the common value of the intensive variable that
labels it is the temperature. With $k_B = 1$, $T$ has units of energy.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The ideal gas is the system to which every definition of this chapter is first applied. Its equation of state is
the low-density limit of every real gas, and it is the equation that the statistical mechanics of @sec-partition-functions
will derive from first principles.

::: {#exm-thd-ideal-gas-state}
#### The ideal gas

A dilute gas of $N$ molecules obeys $pV = NT$ (in SI units $pV = Nk_BT$, with $k_B = 1.380649\times10^{-23}$ J/K).
The state is fixed by any two of $p, V, T$ at given $N$: at $T = 300$ K and $p = 1.013\times10^5$ Pa, one mole
($N = 6.022\times10^{23}$) occupies $V = Nk_BT/p = 2.46\times10^{-2}$ m$^3$, about $24.6$ litres. The
isotherms $p = NT/V$ are hyperbolas in the $p$-$V$ plane, drawn dashed in @fig-carnot-cycle.
:::

Whether a variable is extensive or intensive is a statement about scaling, and it constrains the form of every
equation of state. The second example tests the ideal gas against the definition and draws the consequence for the
functions that may appear in it.

::: {#exm-thd-extensive-intensive}
#### Scaling of state variables

Joining two copies of the same gas doubles $V$ and $N$ and leaves $p$ and $T$ unchanged, so $p = NT/V$ must be a
function of $T$ and the density $N/V$ only, which it is. In general an intensive function $g(V, N)$ satisfies
$g(\lambda V, \lambda N) = g(V, N)$ for all $\lambda > 0$; choosing $\lambda = 1/N$ gives $g(V, N) = g(V/N, 1)$, a
function of the specific volume $v = V/N$ alone. An extensive function satisfies $U(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N) =
\lambda U(S, V, N)$: it is homogeneous of degree one.
:::

Real gases deviate from $pV = NT$ because molecules occupy space and attract each other. Van der Waals' equation
captures both effects with two constants, and it is the simplest equation of state with a liquid-gas transition and
a critical point.

::: {#exm-thd-van-der-waals}
#### The van der Waals gas

The **van der Waals equation** is $\left(p + \frac{aN^2}{V^2}\right)(V - Nb) = NT$, with $b$ the volume excluded by
one molecule and $a > 0$ measuring the attraction. For $V \gg Nb$ and $aN/V \ll T$ it reduces to the ideal gas. Its
isotherms $p = \frac{NT}{V - Nb} - \frac{aN^2}{V^2}$ are monotonic at high $T$ and develop a local maximum and
minimum below the **critical temperature** $T_c = 8a/(27b)$, where $\partial p/\partial V > 0$ on part of the curve,
a mechanically unstable region that signals the coexistence of liquid and gas (@exr-thd-vdw-critical).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The response of a state to small changes is measured by derivatives of the equation of state, and these are the
quantities that experiments measure. The first exercise computes two of them for the ideal gas and proves the
cyclic relation that links the three partial derivatives of any equation of state.

::: {#exr-thd-compressibility}
#### Compressibility and expansion coefficient

For the ideal gas compute the isothermal compressibility $\kappa_T = -\frac1V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial
p}\right)_T$ and the expansion coefficient $\alpha = \frac1V\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_p$. Show that
for any equation of state $g(p, V, T) = 0$, $\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial
T}{\partial V}\right)_p \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial p}\right)_T = -1$, and check it in Sage for the ideal and
van der Waals gases.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $V = NT/p$: $\kappa_T = 1/p$ and $\alpha = 1/T$. By implicit differentiation $\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial
T}\right)_V = -g_T/g_p$, $\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_p = -g_V/g_T$, $\left(\frac{\partial
V}{\partial p}\right)_T = -g_p/g_V$, and the product of the three is $(-1)^3 = -1$:

{{< sage exr-thd-compressibility >}}
:::

A state variable is a function on the space of equilibrium states, and an independent set of them is a coordinate
system on it. The second exercise makes the counting precise for the ideal gas and shows that the choice of
coordinates is free.

::: {#exr-thd-coordinates}
#### Coordinates on the state space

For $N$ fixed, the equilibrium states of an ideal gas form a two-dimensional set. Show that $(p, V)$, $(T, V)$ and
$(p, T)$ are each a valid pair of coordinates on $\{p > 0, V > 0\}$, write the transition maps between them, and
compute the Jacobian determinant $\partial(p, V)/\partial(T, V)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $pV = NT$ each pair determines the third variable: $T = pV/N$, $p = NT/V$, $V = NT/p$, all smooth with smooth
inverses on the positive quadrant, so the three pairs are charts of the same two-dimensional manifold. The map
$(T, V) \mapsto (p, V) = (NT/V, V)$ has Jacobian determinant $\partial p/\partial T|_V = N/V > 0$, and its inverse
is $(p, V) \mapsto (pV/N, V)$. The state space of a simple fluid is a two-dimensional manifold, and thermodynamics
is calculus on it.
:::

The van der Waals isotherms change shape at one temperature, where the maximum and minimum of $p(V)$ merge into an
inflection point. The last exercise locates that critical point and rewrites the equation in units of the critical
values, where the constants $a, b$ disappear.

::: {#exr-thd-vdw-critical}
#### The van der Waals critical point

Find the critical point of the van der Waals gas, where $(\partial p/\partial V)_T = (\partial^2 p/\partial V^2)_T =
0$, and show that in the reduced variables $p_r = p/p_c$, $V_r = V/V_c$, $T_r = T/T_c$ the equation of state is
$p_r = \frac{8T_r}{3V_r - 1} - \frac{3}{V_r^2}$, the same for every gas (the **law of corresponding states**).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first condition gives $T = 2aN(V - Nb)^2/V^3$; substituting into the second leaves $V = 3Nb$, so $V_c = 3Nb$,
$T_c = 8a/(27b)$, $p_c = a/(27b^2)$ and $p_cV_c/(NT_c) = 3/8$, a universal ratio (about $0.29$ for real gases):

{{< sage exr-thd-vdw-critical >}}
:::
::::

### The first law

Energy can enter a system as work, when a piston moves, or as heat, when the system touches a hotter body. The first
law says that the sum of the two changes a function of the state, the internal energy, even though neither of them
separately is the change of any state function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-first-law}
#### First law of thermodynamics

Every system has an extensive state variable, the **internal energy** $U$, such that in any process the change of
$U$ equals the heat $Q$ absorbed by the system minus the work $W$ done by it: $\Delta U = Q - W$. For an
infinitesimal **quasi-static** process (a succession of equilibrium states) of a fluid, $dU = \delta Q - \delta W$
with $\delta W = p\,dV$. Here $dU$ is an exact differential, the differential of a function on the state space,
while $\delta Q$ and $\delta W$ are one-forms on the state space that are not exact: the heat and work exchanged
depend on the path, only their difference does not. The **heat capacities** are $C_V = (\delta Q/dT)_V =
(\partial U/\partial T)_V$ and $C_p = (\delta Q/dT)_p$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On an isotherm the energy of an ideal gas does not change, because its energy depends on the temperature only. All
the work done by the gas is then paid for by heat drawn from the surroundings, and the integral of $p\,dV$ is
elementary.

::: {#exm-thd-isothermal-work}
#### Isothermal expansion

For the monatomic ideal gas $U = \frac32NT$ (derived in @sec-partition-functions). Along the isotherm at temperature
$T$ from $V_1$ to $V_2$, $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2}\frac{NT}{V}dV = NT\log(V_2/V_1)$, $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q = W$. For the
first stroke of the cycle in @fig-carnot-cycle ($N = 1$, $T = 2$, $V_1 = 1$, $V_2 = 2$) the gas absorbs $Q = 2\log
2$ and does the same work.
:::

An adiabatic process exchanges no heat, so the first law alone determines how the temperature falls as the gas
expands. The result is a differential equation on the state space whose solutions are the adiabats.

::: {#exm-thd-adiabat}
#### Adiabatic expansion

With $\delta Q = 0$: $\frac32N\,dT = -\frac{NT}{V}dV$, so $\frac{dT}{T} = -\frac23\frac{dV}{V}$ and $TV^{2/3}$ is
constant along the adiabat; with $T = pV/N$ this is $pV^{5/3} = \text{const}$, steeper than the isotherm $pV =
\text{const}$. In general $pV^\gamma$ is constant with $\gamma = C_p/C_V$ (@exr-thd-heat-capacities). The solid
blue curves of @fig-carnot-cycle are two such adiabats (@exr-thd-adiabat).
:::

The third example exhibits the path dependence of heat and work directly. Two routes join the same two states of an
ideal gas, and they exchange different amounts of work with the surroundings although the change of energy is the
same.

::: {#exm-thd-path-dependence}
#### Work depends on the path

Take the ideal gas from $(p, V) = (2, 1)$ to $(1, 2)$ ($N = 1$, both at $T = 2$). Along the isotherm, $W = 2\log2
\approx 1.386$. Along the path that first expands at constant $p = 2$ to $V = 2$ and then cools at constant $V$ to $p
= 1$, $W = 2\cdot(2 - 1) + 0 = 2$; along the reverse corner (cool at $V = 1$ to $p = 1$, then expand at $p = 1$),
$W = 1$. In all three cases $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W$ differs too: $\delta Q$ is not exact.
:::

Whether a one-form is the differential of a function is decided by a test on its coefficients. The next example applies
the test to four simple forms in the plane, the mathematical content of the distinction between $dU$ and $\delta Q$.

::: {#exm-tsb-exact-forms}
#### Exact and inexact forms

A form $\omega = P\,dx + Q\,dy$ on the plane is exact iff $\partial_yP = \partial_xQ$. For $\omega_1 = xy\,dx + y\,dy$, $\partial_y(xy) = x \neq 0$: not exact.
For $\omega_2 = \sin x\cos y\,dx + \sin y\cos x\,dy$ both cross derivatives are $-\sin x\sin y$, and $\omega_2 = dF$ with $F = -\cos x\cos y$. For
$\omega_3 = x^2dx + y^2dy$, $F = (x^3 + y^3)/3$. For $\omega_4 = y^2dx + x^2dy$ the cross derivatives are $2y$ and $2x$: not exact, and its
integral around the unit square $[0, 1]^2$ is $\oint\omega_4 = \int\!\!\int(2x - 2y)\,dx\,dy = 0$ while around the triangle with vertices
$(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ it is $\tfrac13$ [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.7].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::

The three textbook processes of an ideal gas each have their own heat. The next example computes it from the first law,
for later use in cycles.

::: {#exm-tsb-heat-three-processes}
#### Heat in three processes

For $N$ particles of a monatomic ideal gas, $U = \tfrac32NT$ and $pV = NT$. At constant temperature $\Delta U = 0$ and $Q = W = NT\log(V_2/V_1)$;
at constant volume $W = 0$ and $Q = \tfrac32N\,\Delta T$; at constant pressure $W = p\,\Delta V = N\,\Delta T$ and $Q = \tfrac52N\,\Delta T$. The ratio of
the last two is $\gamma = C_p/C_V = \tfrac53$, the exponent of the adiabat of @exm-thd-adiabat [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.2].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Heat capacities are the first thermodynamic quantities computed from microscopic models. The first exercise finds
them for the monatomic ideal gas at constant volume and at constant pressure, and their ratio, which governs
the adiabats.

::: {#exr-thd-heat-capacities}
#### Heat capacities of the ideal gas

For $U = \frac32NT$ and $pV = NT$, compute $C_V$, then $C_p$ from $\delta Q = dU + p\,dV$ at constant $p$, and
$\gamma = C_p/C_V$. Show that the adiabats satisfy $pV^\gamma = \text{const}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C_V = \frac32N$. At constant $p$, $p\,dV = N\,dT$, so $\delta Q = \frac32N\,dT + N\,dT$ and $C_p = \frac52N$;
$\gamma = 5/3$ and $C_p - C_V = N$. On an adiabat $C_V\,dT = -p\,dV$, and $d(pV) = N\,dT$ gives $C_V(p\,dV +
V\,dp)/N = -p\,dV$, that is, $(C_V + N)p\,dV + C_VV\,dp = 0$, or $\gamma\,dV/V + dp/p = 0$: $pV^\gamma$ is constant.
:::

The adiabat was found by separating variables; Sage solves the same equation and computes the work along it. The
second exercise checks that this work equals the loss of internal energy, as the first law demands when no heat
flows.

::: {#exr-thd-adiabat}
#### The adiabat in Sage

Solve $\frac{dT}{dV} = -\frac{2T}{3V}$ with $T(V_1) = T_1$ in Sage, verify that $TV^{2/3}$ and $pV^{5/3}$ are
constant, and show that the work along the adiabat from $V_1$ to $V_2$ is $W = \frac32N(T_1 - T_2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The solution is $T = T_1(V_1/V)^{2/3}$, and $\int_{V_1}^{V_2}NT\,dV/V = \frac32NT_1(1 - (V_1/V_2)^{2/3}) =
\frac32N(T_1 - T_2) = -\Delta U$:

{{< sage exr-thd-adiabat >}}
:::

That $\delta Q$ is not exact is a statement about a one-form on a two-dimensional manifold, and it has a remarkable
remedy: an integrating factor. The last exercise finds it for the ideal gas, and the function it produces is the
entropy of the next subsection.

::: {#exr-thd-inexact}
#### An integrating factor for heat

On the state space of the monatomic ideal gas with coordinates $(T, V)$, $\delta Q = \frac32N\,dT +
\frac{NT}{V}dV$. Show that $\delta Q$ is not closed, hence not exact, and that $\delta Q/T$ is exact; find the
function whose differential it is.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Writing $\delta Q = A\,dT + B\,dV$, closedness requires $\partial A/\partial V = \partial B/\partial T$; here $0 \neq
N/V$. For $\delta Q/T = \frac{3N}{2T}dT + \frac NVdV$ the two cross derivatives both vanish, and $\delta Q/T =
d\left(\frac32N\log T + N\log V\right)$. The function $S = \frac32N\log T + N\log V + \text{const}$ is the entropy of
the ideal gas (@exm-thd-entropy-ideal-gas), and $1/T$ is the integrating factor that the second law guarantees for
every system.
:::

Because heat is not a state function, a cycle can absorb heat. The next exercise takes an ideal gas around a cycle of
three of the processes of @exm-tsb-heat-three-processes and computes the net heat.

::: {#exr-tsb-cycle}
#### A three-step cycle

An ideal gas of $N$ particles at $(T_1, V_1)$ is heated at constant pressure to $T_2 > T_1$, cooled at constant volume back to $T_1$, and
compressed at constant temperature to $V_1$. Compute the net heat absorbed and the net work done in the cycle, and the same for
the reversed cycle. What would the net heat be if $\delta Q$ were exact? [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.3]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The constant-pressure step ends at $V_2 = V_1T_2/T_1$ and absorbs $\tfrac52N(T_2 - T_1)$; the constant-volume step gives off $\tfrac32N(T_2 - T_1)$; the
isothermal compression gives off $NT_1\log(V_2/V_1) = NT_1\log(T_2/T_1)$. The net heat is $Q = N(T_2 - T_1) - NT_1\log(T_2/T_1) = NT_1(x - 1 - \log x)$,
$x = T_2/T_1$, positive for $x \neq 1$, and equals the net work since $\Delta U = 0$. The reversed cycle has $Q = W < 0$. If $\delta Q$ were exact
its integral around any closed path would vanish: the cycle shows that it is not.
:::

### Entropy and the second law

Heat flows by itself from hot to cold and never the reverse, and no engine converts heat into work completely. The
second law turns these observations into the existence of a state function that never decreases in an isolated
system. @fig-carnot-cycle shows the reversible cycle that makes the definition concrete, in the $p$-$V$ plane and
in the $T$-$S$ plane where it is a rectangle.

![The Carnot cycle of an ideal monatomic gas ($N = 1$, $\gamma = 5/3$) between $T_h = 2$ and $T_c = 1$. Left, the
$p$-$V$ plane: isothermal expansion $A \to B$ at $T_h$ (red), adiabatic expansion $B \to C$ (blue), isothermal
compression $C \to D$ at $T_c$ (orange) and adiabatic compression $D \to A$; the dashed curves are the full
isotherms, and $V_C = 4\sqrt2$, $V_D = 2\sqrt2$. Right, the same cycle in the $T$-$S$ plane is a rectangle whose
area $(T_h - T_c)\Delta S = \log 2$ is the work done; the efficiency is $1 - T_c/T_h = 1/2$. Generated by
`figures/carnot_cycle.sage`.](figures/carnot_cycle.svg){#fig-carnot-cycle width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-entropy}
#### Entropy

The **second law of thermodynamics** asserts that there is an extensive state variable, the **entropy** $S$, such
that for every quasi-static reversible process $dS = \delta Q_{\text{rev}}/T$, where $T$ is the absolute temperature,
and for every process of a thermally isolated system $\Delta S \geq 0$, with equality only for reversible processes
(**Clausius**). Equivalently, $1/T$ is an integrating factor for $\delta Q_{\text{rev}}$. Combined with the first
law, the **fundamental relation** $dU = T\,dS - p\,dV + \mu\,dN$ holds between neighbouring equilibrium states, so
$U(S, V, N)$ determines everything: $T = (\partial U/\partial S)_{V,N}$, $p = -(\partial U/\partial V)_{S,N}$ and the
**chemical potential** $\mu = (\partial U/\partial N)_{S,V}$; inverting, $1/T = (\partial S/\partial U)_{V,N}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The integrating factor of @exr-thd-inexact already produced the entropy of the ideal gas. The first example states
the result with the particle-number dependence that extensivity requires, and reads off the temperature from it.

::: {#exm-thd-entropy-ideal-gas}
#### Entropy of the ideal gas

Integrating $dS = \frac{3N}{2T}dT + \frac NVdV$ at fixed $N$ and requiring $S$ to be extensive gives $S = N\left(\log
\frac VN + \frac32\log T + s_0\right)$ with a constant $s_0$ (fixed by quantum mechanics in @exm-pfn-ideal-gas-thermo).
Inverting with $U = \frac32NT$: $S = N\left(\log\frac VN + \frac32\log\frac{2U}{3N} + s_0\right)$, and $(\partial
S/\partial U)_V = \frac{3N}{2U} = 1/T$, as the definition requires.
:::

A gas that rushes into a vacuum does no work and absorbs no heat, yet the process is irreversible. Its entropy must
therefore rise, and the change is computed along any reversible path between the same end states.

::: {#exm-thd-free-expansion}
#### Free expansion

An ideal gas expands from $V$ into an evacuated container of total volume $2V$. No work is done and no heat flows,
so $\Delta U = 0$ and $T$ is unchanged. The entropy change is computed along the reversible isotherm with the same
end states: $\Delta S = \int\delta Q_{\text{rev}}/T = N\log 2 > 0$, although $Q = 0$ in the actual process. The
reverse process, all molecules returning to one half, would decrease $S$ and never happens; in @sec-ensembles the
reason becomes a count, $2^N$ times more microstates.
:::

Heat conduction between two bodies is the prototype of an irreversible process. The third example computes the
entropy produced and shows that it is positive whatever the initial temperatures, the inequality of arithmetic and
geometric means in disguise.

::: {#exm-thd-heat-flow}
#### Heat flow between two bodies

Two bodies of equal heat capacity $C$ (constant) at $T_1 \neq T_2$ are brought into contact and isolated. Energy
conservation gives the final temperature $T_f = (T_1 + T_2)/2$, and $\Delta S = C\log\frac{T_f}{T_1} + C\log\frac{T_f}{T_2}
= C\log\frac{(T_1 + T_2)^2}{4T_1T_2}$. Since $(T_1 + T_2)^2 - 4T_1T_2 = (T_1 - T_2)^2 > 0$, $\Delta S > 0$; for
$T_1 = 300$, $T_2 = 400$ and $C = 1$, $\Delta S = 0.0206$ (@exr-thd-mixing).
:::

A Carnot cycle needs only the two heats exchanged on its isotherms. The next example evaluates them for one mole of
gas, with the efficiency of @exr-thd-carnot-efficiency as the check.

::: {#exm-tsb-carnot-mole}
#### A Carnot cycle with one mole

One mole of a monatomic ideal gas runs a Carnot cycle between $T_h = 200\,$K and $T_c = 100\,$K, its volume growing by a factor $4$ on the
hot isotherm; the adiabats $VT^{3/2} = \text{const}$ then force the same factor $4$ on the cold isotherm. The heat absorbed is $Q_h = RT_h\log4 =
8.314 \times 200 \times 1.386\,\mathrm{J} = 2305\,$J, the heat given off $Q_c = RT_c\log4 = 1153\,$J, and the work $W = Q_h - Q_c = 1153\,$J, so the efficiency is
$W/Q_h = \tfrac12 = 1 - T_c/T_h$. The entropy taken from the hot source, $Q_h/T_h = R\log4$, equals that given to the cold one
[@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.8].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Carnot cycle of @fig-carnot-cycle is reversible, so the entropy given up by the hot reservoir equals the entropy
received by the cold one. The first exercise turns this balance into the maximal efficiency of any heat engine.

::: {#exr-thd-carnot-efficiency}
#### Carnot efficiency

An engine operates in a cycle between reservoirs at $T_h > T_c$, absorbing $Q_h$ and rejecting $Q_c$. Using $\Delta
S_{\text{total}} \geq 0$ over a cycle, show that the efficiency $\eta = W/Q_h$ satisfies $\eta \leq 1 - T_c/T_h$, with
equality for a reversible engine. Evaluate it for the cycle of @fig-carnot-cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Over a cycle the working substance returns to its state, so $\Delta S_{\text{total}} = -Q_h/T_h + Q_c/T_c \geq 0$,
that is, $Q_c \geq Q_hT_c/T_h$. With $W = Q_h - Q_c$, $\eta = 1 - Q_c/Q_h \leq 1 - T_c/T_h$. For the cycle of the
figure, $Q_h = 2\log 2$, $Q_c = \log 2$ (the cold isotherm runs between $V_D = 2\sqrt2$ and $V_C = 4\sqrt2$, a ratio
of $2$), $W = \log 2$ and $\eta = 1/2 = 1 - 1/2$, as in @prp-maxwell-relations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/carnot_cycle.sage`).
:::

The fundamental relation turns an entropy function into a complete thermodynamics. The second exercise starts from
the entropy of the ideal gas as a function of $U$ and $V$ and recovers both the energy and the equation of state.

::: {#exr-thd-temperature-from-entropy}
#### Equations of state from the entropy

Given $S(U, V) = N\left(\frac32\log U + \log V\right) + \text{const}$ at fixed $N$, use $1/T = (\partial S/\partial
U)_V$ and $p/T = (\partial S/\partial V)_U$ to derive $U = \frac32NT$ and $pV = NT$. Show that $S$ is concave in $U$
and explain why concavity is needed for stability.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $dU = T\,dS - p\,dV$, $dS = dU/T + (p/T)dV$. Then $1/T = 3N/(2U)$ and $p/T = N/V$. Concavity: $\partial^2S/
\partial U^2 = -3N/(2U^2) < 0$. If $S$ were convex somewhere, splitting the energy unequally between two halves of the
system would increase the total entropy $S(U/2 + \epsilon) + S(U/2 - \epsilon) > 2S(U/2)$, and the uniform state
would be unstable. Concavity also gives $\partial T/\partial U = -T^2\partial^2S/\partial U^2 > 0$, a positive heat
capacity.
:::

Mixing two different gases is irreversible in the same way as heat conduction. The last exercise computes the
entropy produced in both processes with Sage and locates the maximum of the mixing entropy.

::: {#exr-thd-mixing}
#### Entropy production in Sage

(a) For @exm-thd-heat-flow, show in Sage that $e^{\Delta S/C} - 1 = (T_1 - T_2)^2/(4T_1T_2)$. (b) $Nx$ molecules of
gas $A$ in volume $xV$ and $N(1 - x)$ molecules of a different gas $B$ in $(1 - x)V$, at equal $T$ and $p$, are
allowed to mix. Show that $\Delta S_{\text{mix}} = -N(x\log x + (1 - x)\log(1 - x))$ and that it is largest at $x =
1/2$, where it equals $N\log 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) follows from $\Delta S = C\log((T_1 + T_2)^2/(4T_1T_2))$. (b) Each gas expands isothermally into the full
volume, $\Delta S_A = Nx\log(1/x)$, $\Delta S_B = N(1 - x)\log(1/(1 - x))$; the derivative $N\log((1 - x)/x)$
vanishes at $x = 1/2$ and the second derivative $-N/(x(1 - x))$ is negative:

{{< sage exr-thd-mixing >}}
:::

The fundamental relation can be reconstructed from the equations of state. The next exercise does this with Sage for
the system that turns out to be black-body radiation.

::: {#exr-tsb-fundamental}
#### The fundamental relation of radiation

A system obeys $E = aVT^4$ and $p = E/(3V)$. Find $S(E, V)$ by integrating $dS = dE/T + p\,dV/T$, check it with Sage, and find its adiabats
[@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.12].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1/T = (aV/E)^{1/4}$ and $p/T = \tfrac13a^{1/4}E^{3/4}V^{-3/4}$ are the partial derivatives of $S = \tfrac43a^{1/4}V^{1/4}E^{3/4}$ (no constant, since $S = 0$ at
$E = 0$):

{{< sage exr-tsb-fundamental >}}

In terms of $T$, $S = \tfrac43aVT^3$, so the adiabats are $VT^3 = \text{const}$, equivalently $pV^{4/3} = \text{const}$: radiation is a gas with
$\gamma = \tfrac43$, as for the radiation-filled expanding universe of general relativity (@exm-gr-friedmann-radiation).
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Thermodynamic potentials

The energy $U(S, V, N)$ is natural when entropy and volume are controlled, but in the laboratory one controls the
temperature and the pressure. Replacing a variable by its conjugate is a Legendre transform, and each choice of
controlled variables has its own potential whose minimum gives the equilibrium.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-thermodynamic-potential}
#### Thermodynamic potential

The **thermodynamic potentials** are the Legendre transforms of $U(S, V, N)$ with respect to some of its arguments:
the **Helmholtz free energy** $F = U - TS$ with $dF = -S\,dT - p\,dV + \mu\,dN$, natural variables $(T, V, N)$; the
**enthalpy** $H = U + pV$ with $dH = T\,dS + V\,dp + \mu\,dN$; the **Gibbs free energy** $G = U - TS + pV$ with $dG
= -S\,dT + V\,dp + \mu\,dN$; and the **grand potential** $\Phi = U - TS - \mu N$ with $d\Phi = -S\,dT - p\,dV -
N\,d\mu$. Each potential, as a function of its natural variables, contains the full thermodynamics, and at fixed
natural variables the equilibrium state of a system in contact with the corresponding reservoirs minimises it
(@exr-thd-minimum-principle).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Helmholtz free energy is the potential of statistical mechanics, since the canonical ensemble will give it
directly as $-T\log Z$. The first example computes it for the ideal gas and recovers pressure and entropy as its
derivatives.

::: {#exm-thd-helmholtz-ideal}
#### Free energy of the ideal gas

With $U = \frac32NT$ and the entropy of @exm-thd-entropy-ideal-gas, $F = U - TS = -NT\left(\log\frac VN + \frac32\log T +
c\right)$ with $c = s_0 - \frac32$. Then $p = -(\partial F/\partial V)_T = NT/V$, $S = -(\partial F/\partial T)_V
= N(\log\frac VN + \frac32\log T + c + \frac32)$, and $U = F + TS = \frac32NT$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/carnot_cycle.sage`).
:::

The Legendre transform replaces a convex function by a function of its slope. The second example performs it
explicitly on the energy of the ideal gas at fixed volume and shows why the minimum over the entropy gives the free
energy.

::: {#exm-thd-legendre}
#### The Legendre transform

At fixed $V, N$ the ideal-gas energy as a function of entropy is $U(S) = Ae^{2S/(3N)}$ with $A > 0$, a convex
function. Its Legendre transform is $F(T) = \min_S\,(U(S) - TS)$: the minimum is where $U'(S) = T$, that is,
$\frac{2A}{3N}e^{2S/(3N)} = T$, so $U = \frac32NT$ and $S = \frac{3N}{2}\log\frac{3NT}{2A}$, and $F(T) = \frac32NT -
\frac32NT\log\frac{3NT}{2A}$. Differentiating, $-F'(T) = \frac32N\log\frac{3NT}{2A} = S$, so the transform is
inverted by the same operation.
:::

Extensivity is a strong constraint: a function homogeneous of degree one equals the sum of its arguments times its
partial derivatives. For the energy this gives the Euler relation and identifies the Gibbs free energy per particle
with the chemical potential.

::: {#exm-thd-gibbs-duhem}
#### Euler and Gibbs-Duhem relations

Differentiating $U(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N) = \lambda U(S, V, N)$ at $\lambda = 1$ gives the **Euler
relation** $U = TS - pV + \mu N$. Hence $G = U - TS + pV = \mu N$: the chemical potential is the Gibbs energy per
particle, and $\Phi = -pV$. Comparing $dU$ from the Euler relation with the fundamental relation gives the
**Gibbs-Duhem relation** $S\,dT - V\,dp + N\,d\mu = 0$: the three intensive variables are not independent.
:::

A free energy of the simplest power-law form already describes a real system. The next example extracts everything
from $F = -CVT^4$, the free energy of black-body radiation derived in @def-blackbody-radiation.

::: {#exm-tsb-photon-free-energy}
#### Thermodynamics from $F = -CVT^4$

With $F(T, V) = -CVT^4$ and no particle number: $S = -\partial_TF = 4CVT^3$, $p = -\partial_VF = CT^4$, $U = F + TS = 3CVT^4 = 3pV$. The pressure depends on
$T$ only, so the isotherms are horizontal in the $(V, p)$ plane, as for a vapour in equilibrium with its liquid, and the chemical
potential, if one is defined by counting photons, vanishes: $G = F + pV = 0$. The adiabats are $VT^3 = \text{const}$
[@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.5].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The enthalpy is the natural potential for processes at constant pressure, such as chemical reactions in an open
vessel. The first exercise derives its differential and shows that it plays the role for $C_p$ that the energy plays
for $C_V$.

::: {#exr-thd-enthalpy}
#### Enthalpy

Derive $dH = T\,dS + V\,dp + \mu\,dN$ from the fundamental relation, show that $C_p = (\partial H/\partial T)_p$,
and compute $H$ and $C_p$ for the monatomic ideal gas.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dH = dU + p\,dV + V\,dp = T\,dS + V\,dp + \mu\,dN$. At constant $p$ and $N$, $dH = T\,dS = \delta Q_{\text{rev}}$, so
$C_p = (\partial H/\partial T)_p$. For the ideal gas $H = \frac32NT + NT = \frac52NT$ and $C_p = \frac52N$, in
agreement with @exr-thd-heat-capacities.
:::

The minimum principle explains why the free energy, and not the energy, decides equilibrium at fixed temperature:
the reservoir's entropy enters. The second exercise derives it from the second law applied to system plus reservoir.

::: {#exr-thd-minimum-principle}
#### The free energy is minimal at equilibrium

A system at fixed $V, N$ is in contact with a large reservoir at temperature $T$. Show that in any spontaneous
process $\Delta F \leq 0$, where $F = U - TS$ is evaluated for the system, so that equilibrium minimises $F$. State
the analogous principle for $G$ at fixed $T$ and $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The reservoir absorbs heat $-\Delta U$ at fixed temperature $T$, so its entropy changes by $-\Delta U/T$. The second
law for the isolated whole gives $\Delta S - \Delta U/T \geq 0$, that is, $\Delta(U - TS) \leq 0$. At fixed $T$ and
$p$ the reservoir also does work: it absorbs heat $-(\Delta U + p\Delta V)$, and the same argument gives $\Delta(U -
TS + pV) = \Delta G \leq 0$. This is why phase coexistence at fixed $T, p$ requires equal Gibbs energy per particle,
$\mu_{\text{liquid}} = \mu_{\text{gas}}$.
:::

For the ideal gas every potential is explicit, so the Euler relation and the Gibbs-Duhem relation can be checked
symbolically. The last exercise does this in Sage starting from the energy as a function of entropy, volume and
particle number.

::: {#exr-thd-euler}
#### Euler relation in Sage

For $U(S, V, N) = \frac32N(N/V)^{2/3}e^{2S/(3N) - s_0}$ compute $T$, $p$ and $\mu$, verify $pV = NT$, $U = TS - pV +
\mu N$, $G = \mu N$, and the Gibbs-Duhem relation along variations of each of $S, V, N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T = (N/V)^{2/3}e^{2S/(3N) - s_0}$, so $U = \frac32NT$; all identities hold exactly:

{{< sage exr-thd-euler >}}
:::

Every thermodynamic potential is a Legendre transform. The next exercise computes two transforms explicitly, to see the
convex duality at work outside physics.

::: {#exr-tsb-legendre}
#### Two Legendre transforms

Compute $f^*(p) = \sup_x(px - f(x))$ for $f(x) = x^\alpha$ on $x > 0$ with $\alpha > 1$, and for $f(x) = e^x$. Check that $f^{**} = f$ in both cases
[@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.9].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $x^\alpha$ the supremum is at $p = \alpha x^{\alpha - 1}$, $x = (p/\alpha)^{1/(\alpha - 1)}$, giving $f^*(p) = (\alpha - 1)(p/\alpha)^{\alpha/(\alpha - 1)}$ for $p > 0$: a power
with the conjugate exponent $\beta = \alpha/(\alpha - 1)$, $1/\alpha + 1/\beta = 1$. For $e^x$ the supremum is at $x = \log p$, giving $f^*(p) = p\log p - p$ for
$p > 0$ ($f^*(0) = 0$, $+\infty$ for $p < 0$): the function $p\log p$ of the entropy. Transforming again, $\sup_p(xp - p\log p + p)$ is attained at
$\log p = x$ and equals $e^x$; similarly for the power. Both functions are convex and the transform is an involution on convex
functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Maxwell relations

A potential is a function of two (or three) variables, and its mixed second derivatives do not depend on the order
of differentiation. Applied to the four potentials, this gives four identities between response functions, the
Maxwell relations, which relate quantities that look unrelated, such as an entropy derivative and a pressure
derivative.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-maxwell-relations}
#### Maxwell relations and checks

For a simple fluid at fixed $N$, the equalities of mixed second derivatives of $U(S, V)$, $H(S, p)$, $F(T, V)$ and
$G(T, p)$ give the **Maxwell relations**
$$
\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S = -\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial S}\right)_V, \quad
\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial p}\right)_S = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\right)_p, \quad
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\right)_V, \quad
\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial p}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_p.
$$
Moreover: (a) $F = -NT(\log(V/N) + \frac32\log T + c)$ gives $pV = NT$, $U = \frac32NT$ and $(\partial S/\partial
V)_T = (\partial p/\partial T)_V = N/V$; (b) the van der Waals free energy $F = F_{\text{ideal}}(V - Nb) - aN^2/V$
gives its equation of state and the critical point $T_c = 8a/(27b)$, $V_c = 3Nb$, $p_c = a/(27b^2)$; (c) on the
Carnot cycle of the ideal monatomic gas $TV^{2/3}$ is constant on the adiabats, the entropy change over the cycle is
zero and the efficiency is $1 - T_c/T_h$; (d) $C_p - C_V = -T(\partial p/\partial T)_V^2/(\partial p/\partial V)_T$,
which is $N$ for the ideal gas and $N/(1 - 2aN(V - Nb)^2/(TV^3))$ for van der Waals; (e) the Euler relation $U = TS -
pV + \mu N$ holds for the ideal gas.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/carnot_cycle.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The third Maxwell relation turns an entropy derivative, which no instrument measures, into a pressure derivative
read off the equation of state. The first example checks it on the ideal gas, the second uses it to find how energy
depends on volume.

::: {#exm-thd-maxwell-ideal}
#### Maxwell relation for the ideal gas

From $F$ in (a), $S = -\partial F/\partial T$ and $p = -\partial F/\partial V$, and $\partial S/\partial V = -\partial^2
F/\partial V\partial T = \partial p/\partial T$; both equal $N/V$. Along an isotherm the entropy therefore grows as
$N\log V$, in agreement with the free expansion of @exm-thd-free-expansion.
:::

Whether the energy of a gas depends on its volume at fixed temperature is a question about molecular attraction.
The Maxwell relation answers it from the equation of state alone, and the answer distinguishes the ideal gas from van
der Waals.

::: {#exm-thd-energy-equation}
#### The energy equation

From $dU = T\,dS - p\,dV$ at fixed $T$: $(\partial U/\partial V)_T = T(\partial S/\partial V)_T - p = T(\partial
p/\partial T)_V - p$. For the ideal gas this is $T\cdot N/V - p = 0$: the energy depends on $T$ only. For the van der
Waals gas $T(\partial p/\partial T)_V - p = aN^2/V^2$, so $U = \frac32NT - aN^2/V$; the attraction lowers the energy
of the denser state (@exr-thd-vdw-energy).
:::

The two heat capacities differ because heating at constant pressure also does expansion work. The third example
evaluates the general formula of (d) for the ideal gas, where the difference is the number of particles.

::: {#exm-thd-cp-cv}
#### The difference of heat capacities

Writing $S(T, V)$ and changing variables, $C_p - C_V = T(\partial S/\partial V)_T(\partial V/\partial T)_p$, and
the Maxwell relation and the cyclic rule of @exr-thd-compressibility turn this into $-T(\partial p/\partial T)_V^2/
(\partial p/\partial V)_T = TV\alpha^2/\kappa_T$. For the ideal gas $TV(1/T)^2/(1/p) = pV/T = N$. Since $\kappa_T > 0$
for a stable system, $C_p \geq C_V$ always.
:::

The grand potential has Maxwell relations of its own. The next example derives them, since they are the ones used for
open systems such as the grand-canonical ensemble.

::: {#exm-tsb-grand-maxwell}
#### Maxwell relations of the grand potential

From $d\Phi = -S\,dT - p\,dV - N\,d\mu$ (@def-thermodynamic-potential) the equality of mixed derivatives gives
$$
\Bigl(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\Bigr)_{T,\mu} = \Bigl(\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}\Bigr)_{V,\mu}, \quad \Bigl(\frac{\partial S}{\partial\mu}\Bigr)_{T,V} = \Bigl(\frac{\partial N}{\partial T}\Bigr)_{V,\mu}, \quad
\Bigl(\frac{\partial p}{\partial\mu}\Bigr)_{T,V} = \Bigl(\frac{\partial N}{\partial V}\Bigr)_{T,\mu} .
$$
For an extensive system $\Phi = -pV$ and $N = V\,(\partial p/\partial\mu)_T$, so the last relation reads $n = (\partial p/\partial\mu)_T$, the Gibbs-Duhem
relation of @exm-thd-gibbs-duhem at constant temperature [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.6].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Each potential gives one Maxwell relation, and the Gibbs free energy gives the one used most in chemistry, since $T$
and $p$ are its variables. The first exercise derives it and checks it on the ideal gas.

::: {#exr-thd-maxwell-gibbs}
#### The Maxwell relation of the Gibbs energy

From $dG = -S\,dT + V\,dp$ derive $(\partial S/\partial p)_T = -(\partial V/\partial T)_p$ and verify it for the
ideal gas, with $S(T, p)$ obtained from @exm-thd-entropy-ideal-gas by substituting $V = NT/p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial^2G/\partial T\partial p = \partial^2G/\partial p\partial T$ gives $-(\partial S/\partial p)_T =
(\partial V/\partial T)_p$. With $V = NT/p$, $S = N(\log(T/p) + \frac32\log T + \text{const}) = N(\frac52\log T -
\log p) + \text{const}$, so $(\partial S/\partial p)_T = -N/p$, and $(\partial V/\partial T)_p = N/p$.
:::

Gas forced slowly through a porous plug at constant enthalpy cools or warms depending on whether attraction or
repulsion dominates; this is how gases are liquefied. The second exercise derives the Joule-Thomson coefficient with a
Maxwell relation.

::: {#exr-thd-joule-thomson}
#### The Joule-Thomson coefficient

Show that $\mu_{JT} = (\partial T/\partial p)_H = \frac{T(\partial V/\partial T)_p - V}{C_p}$, that it vanishes for
the ideal gas, and that for the van der Waals gas at low density, $V \gg Nb$, it is approximately $\frac{N}{C_p}
\left(\frac{2a}{T} - b\right)$, positive (cooling on expansion) below the inversion temperature $T_{\text{inv}} =
2a/b$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At constant $H$, $0 = dH = T\,dS + V\,dp$, and $dS = (C_p/T)dT + (\partial S/\partial p)_Tdp = (C_p/T)dT - (\partial
V/\partial T)_pdp$ by @exr-thd-maxwell-gibbs; solving, $(\partial T/\partial p)_H = (T(\partial V/\partial T)_p -
V)/C_p$. For $V = NT/p$ the numerator is $NT/p - V = 0$. For van der Waals to first order in $a, b$, $V \approx
NT/p + Nb - aN/T$, so $T(\partial V/\partial T)_p - V \approx (NT/p + aN/T) - (NT/p + Nb - aN/T) = N(2a/T - b)$.
Since $T_{\text{inv}} = 2a/b = \frac{27}{4}T_c$, nitrogen ($T_c = 126$ K) cools on throttling at room temperature
while hydrogen ($T_c = 33$ K) must be precooled.
:::

The energy equation of @exm-thd-energy-equation predicts that a van der Waals gas cools when it expands freely into a
vacuum, unlike the ideal gas. The last exercise checks the energy equation in Sage and computes the temperature drop.

::: {#exr-thd-vdw-energy}
#### Free expansion of a van der Waals gas

With Sage, compute $(\partial U/\partial V)_T$ for the van der Waals gas from the energy equation, verify that $U =
\frac32NT - aN^2/V$ satisfies it, and find the final temperature after a free expansion from $V_1$ to $V_2 > V_1$
at constant $U$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\partial U/\partial V)_T = aN^2/V^2$, and at constant $U$: $T_2 - T = -\frac{2aN}{3}\left(\frac1{V_1} -
\frac1{V_2}\right) < 0$, a cooling that vanishes with the attraction $a$:

{{< sage exr-thd-vdw-energy >}}
:::

A fundamental relation $U(S, V, N)$ gives the equations of state by differentiation. The next exercise does this for a
simple homogeneous example and checks the first Maxwell relation on it.

::: {#exr-tsb-equations-of-state}
#### Equations of state from $U(S, V, N)$

For $U = aS^3/(NV)$ with $a > 0$, find $T(s, v)$ and $p(s, v)$ in terms of $s = S/N$ and $v = V/N$, check $(\partial T/\partial V)_S = -(\partial p/\partial S)_V$,
and show that $U$ is extensive [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 5.11].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T = \partial_SU = 3aS^2/(NV) = 3as^2/v$ and $p = -\partial_VU = aS^3/(NV^2) = as^3/v^2$. Then $\partial_VT = -3aS^2/(NV^2)$ and $\partial_Sp = 3aS^2/(NV^2)$, so the
relation holds, as it must for the mixed derivatives of one function. $U(\lambda S, \lambda V, \lambda N) = \lambda U$: per particle $u = as^3/v$, and
$T$ and $p$ depend on $(s, v)$ only, as intensive variables should.
:::

## Statistical ensembles {#sec-ensembles}

Statistical mechanics explains thermodynamics by counting. A macroscopic state is compatible with an enormous number
of microscopic states, and an ensemble is a probability measure on them (@def-probability-measure); the
thermodynamic variables are expectations (@def-expectation), and their fluctuations are variances
(@def-variance) that become negligible for large systems. This section defines the microcanonical ensemble of an
isolated system, the canonical ensemble of a system at fixed temperature with its partition function and Boltzmann
distribution, and the grand-canonical ensemble of a system that also exchanges particles, together with the identities that relate
their partition functions to the thermodynamic variables.

### Microstates and the microcanonical ensemble

A microstate is a complete microscopic description, the quantum state of every particle or a point in phase space,
and a macrostate fixes only the energy, volume and particle number. The fundamental postulate assigns equal
probability to all microstates of an isolated system with the given energy, and the logarithm of their number is the
entropy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-microcanonical-ensemble}
#### Microcanonical ensemble

Let a system have a discrete set of **microstates** $i$ with energies $E_i$, and let $\Omega(E, V, N)$ be the number
of microstates with energy $E$ (in practice, in a narrow window $[E, E + \delta E]$). The **microcanonical ensemble**
is the uniform probability measure on these microstates, $p_i = 1/\Omega(E)$ (**equal a priori probabilities**). The
**Boltzmann entropy** is $S(E, V, N) = \log\Omega(E, V, N)$ (in SI units $k_B\log\Omega$), and the temperature,
pressure and chemical potential are defined by the fundamental relation of @def-entropy: $\frac1T =
\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}$, $\frac pT = \frac{\partial S}{\partial V}$, $\frac\mu T = -\frac{\partial S}{\partial
N}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest system with many microstates is a row of spins that can point up or down. Counting its microstates is
a binomial coefficient, and Stirling's formula turns its logarithm into the entropy of mixing seen in the last section.

::: {#exm-ens-spins}
#### Two-state spins

$N$ independent spins, each of energy $0$ (down) or $\epsilon$ (up), with $n$ up: $E = n\epsilon$ and $\Omega =
\binom Nn$. By Stirling's formula $\log N! = N\log N - N + O(\log N)$, $S = \log\binom Nn \approx -N\left(x\log x +
(1 - x)\log(1 - x)\right)$ with $x = n/N$, the curve on the right of @fig-boltzmann-distribution; the maximum $S =
N\log 2$ is at $x = 1/2$, and $0 \leq NH(x) - \log\binom Nn \leq \log(N + 1)$ for $N = 100$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/boltzmann_distribution.sage`).
:::

Einstein's model of a solid replaces each atom by three harmonic oscillators that share quanta of energy. The number of
ways to distribute the quanta is the classic stars-and-bars count, and it grows so fast that two such solids in
contact almost certainly share energy in proportion to their sizes.

::: {#exm-ens-einstein-solid}
#### The Einstein solid

$N$ oscillators share $q$ indistinguishable energy quanta $\hbar\omega$; a microstate is a sequence $(n_1, \dots,
n_N)$ of non-negative integers with sum $q$, and $\Omega(N, q) = \binom{q + N - 1}{q}$ (@exr-ens-stars-bars). For $N
= 3$, $q = 2$: $\Omega = \binom42 = 6$, the states $(2,0,0), (0,2,0), (0,0,2), (1,1,0), (1,0,1), (0,1,1)$. For $q, N
\gg 1$, $S \approx (q + N)\log(q + N) - q\log q - N\log N$.
:::

Two systems that can exchange energy share it in the way that maximises the number of joint microstates. Since the
logarithm is increasing, this is the way that maximises the total entropy, and the condition for the maximum is the
equality of the temperatures defined above.

::: {#exm-ens-thermal-contact}
#### Thermal contact

Systems $A$ and $B$ with total energy $E$ have $\Omega(E_A) = \Omega_A(E_A)\Omega_B(E - E_A)$ joint microstates
with $A$ at energy $E_A$. The most probable $E_A$ maximises $S_A(E_A) + S_B(E - E_A)$, where $\partial S_A/\partial
E_A = \partial S_B/\partial E_B$, that is, $T_A = T_B$: the zeroth law. For two Einstein solids with $N_A = 300$,
$N_B = 200$ and $q = 100$ the most probable $q_A$ is $60$, the standard deviation is $5.4$, and the probability of
$q_A \leq 30$ is $3\times10^{-8}$ (@exr-ens-sharp-peak); the peak sharpens as $1/\sqrt N$.
:::

Counting arrangements gives the thermodynamics of point defects in a crystal. The next example uses the counting of
@prp-ensemble-identities (c) for atoms that leave their lattice sites.

::: {#exm-tsb-defects}
#### Defects in a crystal

Let $n$ of the $N$ atoms of a crystal be displaced to the surface at an energy cost $\epsilon$ each, so $E = E_0 + n\epsilon$ and $\Omega = \binom Nn$. With
Stirling's formula $S = -N[x\log x + (1 - x)\log(1 - x)]$, $x = n/N$, and $1/T = \partial S/\partial E = \epsilon^{-1}\log\frac{N - n}{n}$, hence
$$
\frac nN = \frac{1}{e^{\epsilon/T} + 1} \approx e^{-\epsilon/T} .
$$
For $\epsilon = 1\,$eV at $T = 1000\,$K ($0.0862\,$eV), $n/N \approx e^{-11.6} = 9 \times 10^{-6}$; at room temperature $e^{-38.7} \approx 10^{-17}$
[@bricmont2022statistical, Exercise 6.9].
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The count of the Einstein solid is the number of ways to place $q$ indistinguishable balls in $N$ boxes. The first
exercise proves it by the stars-and-bars argument and computes the temperature of the solid.

::: {#exr-ens-stars-bars}
#### Stars and bars

Show that the number of $N$-tuples of non-negative integers with sum $q$ is $\binom{q + N - 1}{q}$. Using Stirling's
formula, compute $1/T = \partial S/\partial E$ with $E = q\hbar\omega$, and show that $q/N = 1/(e^{\hbar\omega/T} -
1)$, the mean occupation of an oscillator.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A tuple corresponds to a row of $q$ stars and $N - 1$ bars (the bars separate the boxes), and choosing which $q$ of
the $q + N - 1$ positions are stars gives the count. With $S \approx (q + N)\log(q + N) - q\log q - N\log N$,
$\partial S/\partial q = \log\frac{q + N}{q}$, so $\frac{\hbar\omega}{T} = \log\left(1 + \frac Nq\right)$ and $q/N =
1/(e^{\hbar\omega/T} - 1)$: the Bose-Einstein occupation at $\mu = 0$ (@exm-pfn-oscillator-energy), here derived
without the canonical ensemble.
:::

The spin system has a bounded energy, and that has a strange consequence: its entropy decreases when more than
half the spins are up. The second exercise computes its temperature and finds negative values.

::: {#exr-ens-spin-temperature}
#### Negative temperature

For the spins of @exm-ens-spins with $S = N H(n/N)$, compute $1/T = \partial S/\partial E$ and show $n/N =
1/(e^{\epsilon/T} + 1)$. What is $T$ when $n > N/2$? Explain why a system at negative temperature, put in contact
with any system at positive temperature, gives energy to it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial S/\partial n = \log\frac{N - n}{n}$, so $\epsilon/T = \log\frac{N - n}{n}$ and $n/N = 1/(e^{\epsilon/T} +
1)$. For $n > N/2$ the logarithm is negative: $T < 0$. The
order of hotness is that of $-1/T$: $1/T$ runs from $+\infty$ (cold) through $0$ ($n = N/2$) to $-\infty$ (all up),
and energy flows from the system with smaller $1/T$ to the one with larger $1/T$; any negative $T$ has $1/T < 0 <
1/T'$ for every positive $T'$. Nuclear spin systems in a magnetic field realise this after a field reversal.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/boltzmann_distribution.sage`).
:::

The sharpness of the energy distribution between two systems is the reason thermodynamics is deterministic. The last
exercise computes the distribution exactly with Sage's big integers.

::: {#exr-ens-sharp-peak}
#### A sharp maximum

Two Einstein solids with $N_A = 300$, $N_B = 200$ share $q = 100$ quanta. With Sage, compute the probability
$P(q_A) = \Omega_A(q_A)\Omega_B(q - q_A)/\Omega(N_A + N_B, q)$, check the normalisation, and find the most probable
value, the mean, the standard deviation and $P(50 \leq q_A \leq 70)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The total count is $\binom{q + N_A + N_B - 1}{q}$ (the two solids together are one solid of $500$ oscillators); the
mean $60 = qN_A/(N_A + N_B)$ is exact by symmetry among the oscillators, and $95\%$ of the probability lies within
$\pm10$:

{{< sage exr-ens-sharp-peak >}}
:::

The microcanonical entropy and the canonical free energy of the same system are Legendre transforms of each other.
The next exercise checks this exactly and numerically for independent spins.

::: {#exr-tsb-spin-legendre}
#### Microcanonical and canonical spins

Let $s_i = \pm1$, $i = 1, \dots, N$, with energy $E = \sum_is_i$. Compute $s(e) = \lim\log\Omega(E, N)/N$ at $E/N = e$ and $f(T) = -T\lim\log Z/N$, and show with
Sage that $f(T) = \min_e(e - Ts(e))$ and $s(e) = \min_T(e - f(T))/T$ [@bricmont2022statistical, Exercises 6.3-6.5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Omega = \binom{N}{(N + E)/2}$, and Stirling gives $s(e) = -\tfrac{1 + e}{2}\log\tfrac{1 + e}{2} - \tfrac{1 - e}{2}\log\tfrac{1 - e}{2}$; $Z = (2\cosh\beta)^N$ gives $f(T) =
-T\log(2\cosh(1/T))$:

{{< sage exr-tsb-spin-legendre >}}

The finite-$N$ entropy approaches $s(e)$ with a correction of order $\log N/N$; $s'(e) = -\operatorname{artanh}e = 1/T$ fixes the energy $e = -\tanh(1/T)$ that
dominates the canonical sum, which is why the two ensembles agree.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### The canonical ensemble

A system in contact with a heat bath does not have a fixed energy; it exchanges energy with the bath, and its
energy is a random variable. The probability of each microstate follows from the microcanonical ensemble of system
plus bath, and the result is the exponential distribution that @fig-boltzmann-distribution plots for three
temperatures.

![Left: the Boltzmann probabilities $p_n = e^{-E_n/T}/Z$ of the equally spaced levels $E_n = n$ at $T = 1/2, 1, 3$;
low temperature concentrates the probability in the ground state, high temperature spreads it over many levels.
Right: the microcanonical entropy per spin $\log\binom Nn/N$ of $N = 100$ two-state spins (dots) against the Stirling
form $-x\log x - (1 - x)\log(1 - x)$ with $x = n/N$; the difference is at most $\log(N + 1)/N$. Generated by
`figures/boltzmann_distribution.sage`.](figures/boltzmann_distribution.svg){#fig-boltzmann-distribution width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-canonical-ensemble}
#### Canonical ensemble

A system with microstates $i$ of energies $E_i$, in thermal contact with a much larger reservoir at temperature $T$,
is described by the **canonical ensemble**, the probability measure
$$
p_i = \frac{e^{-\beta E_i}}{Z}, \qquad \beta = \frac1T, \qquad Z = \sum_i e^{-\beta E_i},
$$
called the **Boltzmann distribution** (or Gibbs distribution); $e^{-\beta E_i}$ is the **Boltzmann factor**. If the
energy level $E$ has $g(E)$ microstates (its **degeneracy**), the probability of the level is $g(E)e^{-\beta E}/Z$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A single spin in contact with a bath is the smallest canonical system. Its two probabilities depend only on the ratio
of the level spacing to the temperature, and the example evaluates them in the two limits.

::: {#exm-ens-two-state}
#### A spin in a heat bath

A two-state system with energies $0$ and $\epsilon$: $Z = 1 + e^{-\beta\epsilon}$, $p_{\text{up}} = 1/(e^{\beta
\epsilon} + 1)$. For $T \ll \epsilon$, $p_{\text{up}} \approx e^{-\epsilon/T} \to 0$; for $T \gg \epsilon$, $p_{\text
{up}} \to 1/2$. At positive temperature the upper state is never more than half occupied, unlike the isolated spins of
@exr-ens-spin-temperature.
:::

The Boltzmann distribution follows from the microcanonical ensemble applied to the system together with its
reservoir. The derivation needs only the definition of temperature and a first-order expansion of the reservoir
entropy.

::: {#exm-ens-reservoir}
#### Derivation from the reservoir

The system in microstate $i$ leaves energy $E_{\text{tot}} - E_i$ to the reservoir, which has $\Omega_R(E_{\text{tot}} -
E_i) = e^{S_R(E_{\text{tot}} - E_i)}$ microstates; by equal a priori probabilities, $p_i \propto \Omega_R$. Since
$E_i \ll E_{\text{tot}}$, $S_R(E_{\text{tot}} - E_i) = S_R(E_{\text{tot}}) - E_i\,\partial S_R/\partial E + \dots =
S_R(E_{\text{tot}}) - E_i/T + \dots$, the higher terms being suppressed by the size of the reservoir. Hence $p_i
\propto e^{-E_i/T}$, and normalisation gives $Z$.
:::

The Boltzmann factor also governs the distribution of molecules in a gravitational field. The third example derives
the barometric formula, a canonical distribution in a continuous variable.

::: {#exm-ens-barometric}
#### The isothermal atmosphere

A molecule of mass $m$ at height $h$ has potential energy $mgh$. In an isothermal atmosphere the probability density
of its height is $p(h) = \frac{mg}{T}e^{-mgh/T}$ on $h \geq 0$, an exponential distribution with mean $T/(mg)$, the
**scale height**: for nitrogen at $T = 288$ K, $T/(mg) = \frac{1.38\times10^{-23}\cdot 288}{4.65\times10^{-26}\cdot 9.
81} \approx 8.7$ km, and the density and pressure fall by $e$ every $8.7$ km.
:::

The canonical distribution is the target of Monte Carlo simulations, which sample it with a Markov chain. The next
example builds the chain of the Metropolis algorithm for a single two-level system.

::: {#exm-tsb-metropolis-two-state}
#### The Metropolis chain of a two-level system

Let the states have energies $0$ and $\epsilon > 0$. The Metropolis rule proposes the other state and accepts it with probability
$\min(1, e^{-\beta\Delta E})$, giving the transition matrix
$$
P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - e^{-\beta\epsilon} & e^{-\beta\epsilon} \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} .
$$
The Boltzmann distribution $w = (1, e^{-\beta\epsilon})/Z$ satisfies $w_0P_{01} = w_1P_{10}$ (detailed balance) and hence $wP = w$. The other
eigenvalue of $P$ is $-e^{-\beta\epsilon}$, so the chain converges to $w$ geometrically, more slowly at high temperature, where it nearly
alternates between the two states [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 7.5.1].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Ratios of Boltzmann probabilities depend only on energy differences, and the partition function cancels. The first
exercise uses this to estimate how many hydrogen atoms in the solar atmosphere are excited.

::: {#exr-ens-ratio}
#### Excited hydrogen in the Sun

The first excited level of hydrogen lies $10.2$ eV above the ground state and has degeneracy $8$ (counting spin; the
ground state has $2$). At the solar surface temperature $T = 5800$ K ($k_BT = 0.500$ eV), estimate the ratio of the
populations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{g_2}{g_1}e^{-(E_2 - E_1)/T} = 4e^{-10.2/0.500} = 4e^{-20.4} \approx 5.5\times10^{-9}$.
Although the temperature is high on human scales, it is small compared with atomic energies, and almost all atoms
are in the ground state; the Balmer absorption lines of the solar spectrum come from this small fraction.
:::

The Boltzmann distribution is also the answer to an optimisation problem: it has the largest entropy among all
distributions with a given mean energy. The second exercise derives it with Lagrange multipliers, and identifies
$\beta$ as the multiplier of the energy constraint.

::: {#exr-ens-max-entropy}
#### Maximum entropy

Maximise the Gibbs entropy $S = -\sum_ip_i\log p_i$ subject to $\sum_ip_i = 1$ and $\sum_ip_iE_i = U$. Show that the
stationary point is the Boltzmann distribution, that it is a maximum, and that $\beta = \partial S/\partial U$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Stationarity of $-\sum p\log p - \alpha\sum p - \beta\sum pE$ gives $-\log p_i - 1 - \alpha - \beta E_i = 0$, so $p_i
= e^{-1-\alpha}e^{-\beta E_i}$, and normalisation fixes $e^{1 + \alpha} = Z$. The Hessian of $S$ is
$\operatorname{diag}(-1/p_i)$, negative definite, so $S$ is strictly concave and the stationary point on the affine
constraint set is the global maximum. At the maximum $S = \beta U + \log
Z$, and $dS/dU = \beta + U\,d\beta/dU + (d\log Z/d\beta)\,d\beta/dU = \beta$, since $d\log Z/d\beta = -U$.
:::

The levels of @fig-boltzmann-distribution form an infinite ladder, and their partition function is a geometric
series. The last exercise sums it in Sage and computes the probabilities plotted in the figure.

::: {#exr-ens-boltzmann-levels}
#### The ladder of levels

For the levels $E_n = n$, $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, compute $Z(\beta)$ and $\langle E\rangle$ exactly in Sage, list
$p_0, \dots, p_3$ at $T = 1/2, 1, 3$, and bound the probability of levels beyond $n = 9$, which the figure omits.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Z = 1/(1 - e^{-\beta})$, $\langle E\rangle = 1/(e^\beta - 1)$, and $P(n \geq 10) = e^{-10\beta}$, at most
$3.6\%$ at $T = 3$:

{{< sage exr-ens-boltzmann-levels >}}
:::

Every Markov chain with a positive power of its transition matrix converges to a unique stationary distribution. The
next exercise computes it for a three-state chain with Sage and asks whether it obeys detailed balance.

::: {#exr-tsb-markov}
#### A three-state Markov chain

For the transition matrix
$$
P = \begin{pmatrix} 3/4 & 1/4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2/3 & 1/3 \\ 1/4 & 1/4 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix},
$$
find with Sage the eigenvalues and right eigenvectors, the stationary distribution $w = wP$ and $\lim_nP^n$. Does $w$ depend on the starting
distribution? Does the chain satisfy detailed balance? [@boudreau2018applied, Ch. 7, Exercise 16]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are $1$, $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac5{12}$; the eigenvector of $1$ is $(1, 1, 1)$, since the rows sum to one:

{{< sage exr-tsb-markov >}}

$P^n \to \mathbf 1w$ with $w = (\tfrac27, \tfrac37, \tfrac27)$, so every initial distribution converges to $w$, at the rate $2^{-n}$ of the second eigenvalue.
Detailed balance fails ($w_1P_{12} = \tfrac1{14} \neq 0 = w_2P_{21}$): the chain has a stationary probability current around the cycle $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1$.
Detailed balance is sufficient for stationarity, not necessary; Monte Carlo algorithms impose it because it is easy to check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The heat bath algorithm replaces the acceptance test by a direct draw from the conditional Boltzmann distribution of
one spin. The next exercise proves that it samples the canonical ensemble.

::: {#exr-tsb-detailed-balance}
#### The heat bath obeys detailed balance

In the Ising model let $E_i$ be the local field on spin $i$, so that the energy is $-\sigma_iE_i$ plus terms not involving $\sigma_i$. The heat bath
(Glauber) update sets $\sigma_i = +1$ with probability $e^{\beta E_i}/(e^{\beta E_i} + e^{-\beta E_i})$, regardless of its old value. Show that this rule,
equivalently $W(\sigma_i \to -\sigma_i) = \tfrac12(1 - \sigma_i\tanh\beta E_i)$, satisfies detailed balance with respect to the Boltzmann distribution
[@boudreau2018applied, Ch. 7, Exercise 13, and Ch. 20, Exercise 17].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $c$ and $c'$ differ only by $\sigma_i \to -\sigma_i$. Then $p(c')/p(c) = e^{-2\beta\sigma_iE_i}$, and $W(c \to c') = e^{-\beta\sigma_iE_i}/(e^{\beta E_i} + e^{-\beta E_i})$,
$W(c' \to c) = e^{\beta\sigma_iE_i}/(e^{\beta E_i} + e^{-\beta E_i})$, whose ratio is $e^{-2\beta\sigma_iE_i}$. Hence $p(c)W(c \to c') = p(c')W(c' \to c)$. Moreover
$e^{-\beta\sigma_iE_i}/(2\cosh\beta E_i) = \tfrac12(1 - \sigma_i\tanh\beta E_i)$, the Glauber form. Together with irreducibility (any configuration can be
reached by single flips) this makes the Boltzmann distribution the unique stationary distribution.
:::

### The partition function

The normalising constant of the Boltzmann distribution is far more than a normalisation. As a function of $\beta$ it
generates all the moments of the energy, and its logarithm is the free energy; the whole thermodynamics of a system
is the computation of one sum.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-partition-function}
#### Partition function

The **canonical partition function** of a system with microstates $i$ of energies $E_i$ is $Z(\beta) = \sum_ie^{-
\beta E_i}$ (a trace $\operatorname{tr}e^{-\beta H}$ in quantum mechanics, an integral over phase space classically).
It determines the **free energy** $F = -T\log Z$, the **mean energy** $U = \langle E\rangle = -\partial\log Z/\partial
\beta$, the **energy variance** $\langle E^2\rangle - \langle E\rangle^2 = \partial^2\log Z/\partial\beta^2$, the *
*heat capacity** $C = \partial U/\partial T = \beta^2\partial^2\log Z/\partial\beta^2$, and the **Gibbs entropy**
$S = -\sum_ip_i\log p_i = \beta U + \log Z$, so that $F = U - TS$ as in @def-thermodynamic-potential. Further
derivatives with respect to external parameters give the corresponding forces, for example $p = -\partial F/\partial
V$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two-level system is the first partition function to compute in full. Every quantity of the definition comes out
in closed form, and the example records the free energy and entropy at low and high temperature.

::: {#exm-ens-z-two-level}
#### Partition function of a two-level system

For energies $0$ and $\epsilon$: $Z = 1 + e^{-\beta\epsilon}$, $F = -T\log(1 + e^{-\epsilon/T})$, $U =
\epsilon/(e^{\beta\epsilon} + 1)$ and $S = \log(1 + e^{-\beta\epsilon}) + \beta\epsilon/(e^{\beta\epsilon} + 1)$. As
$T \to 0$, $F \to 0$ and $S \to 0$; as $T \to \infty$, $F \approx -T\log 2$ and $S \to \log 2$, the logarithm of the
number of states. The heat capacity is the Schottky curve of @sec-partition-functions.
:::

For independent subsystems the Boltzmann factor factorises, and so does the partition function. This is what makes
the free energy extensive, and it is the reason most partition functions in this chapter can be computed at all.

::: {#exm-ens-z-factorise}
#### Independent subsystems

If $E_{(i, j)} = E_i^{(1)} + E_j^{(2)}$ for the microstates $(i, j)$ of two non-interacting systems, then $Z =
\sum_{i,j}e^{-\beta E_i^{(1)}}e^{-\beta E_j^{(2)}} = Z_1Z_2$ and $F = F_1 + F_2$. For $N$ distinguishable identical
subsystems $Z = Z_1^N$ and $F = NF_1$; for $N$ two-level systems $F = -NT\log(1 + e^{-\epsilon/T})$. For
indistinguishable particles the counting changes (@exm-pfn-ideal-gas).
:::

The variance formula has a physical consequence: the heat capacity is a variance, hence never negative. The third
example draws it and estimates the relative size of energy fluctuations in a macroscopic system.

::: {#exm-ens-heat-capacity-fluct}
#### Heat capacity as a variance

From the definition, $C = \beta^2\operatorname{Var}(E) \geq 0$. For $N$ independent systems both $U$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(E)$ are proportional to $N$, so $\Delta E/U \propto 1/\sqrt N$; for $N$ two-level systems
$(\Delta E/U)^2 = e^{\beta\epsilon}/N$ exactly. For $N = 10^{23}$ the relative
fluctuation is about $10^{-11.5}$: the canonical energy is sharp, and the canonical and microcanonical ensembles give
the same thermodynamics, as the law of large numbers of @sec-limit-theorems suggests.
:::
